The “Purlie Victorious” that opened on Wednesday at the Music Box — unaccountably its first Broadway revival — is every bit as scathingly funny as the 1961 reviews said it was.

Young’s hilarious, heartening Lutiebelle fulfills a hope shared by lovers of performance and workers for social peace—that freedom might be found not only on a page but written in a body, and on the heart.
It's a feat to be seen, felt, and enthralled by.
This tale of equity, debts owed and reparations demanded, is a clarion call made loud and clear by Purlie and everyone on the Music Box stage, none more so than the late, great Ossie Davis himself.
The themes of "Purlie Victorious" — segregation, racial terror and the unjustness of sharecropping — are no laughing matter.
The play remains radical today, and for the same reason.
His production, built for speed and farcical flamboyance, threatens to spin out of control but keeps its eye on the prize of social justice.
Almost immediately, it asserts itself as a play that feels contemporary both in its clarity about lingering racism and its willingness to generate big laughs from that very clarity.
The result is an unqualified delight, and a welcome change of pace on Broadway.

Purlie Victorious, running a swift and intermissionless 100 minutes, is theatre for everyone: truly funny, socially meaningful, historically educational, politically progressive, appealingly accessible, emotionally inspiring, and marvelously performed.
Flat-out hilarious and stacked with topflight performances led by Leslie Odom, Jr. and Kara Young, Purlie Victorious is also a triumph when it comes to timing.

Ossie Davis’ Purlie Victorious (A Non-Confederate Romp Through the Cotton Patch) is both uproarious satire and cultural gut punch—with the biggest clue in its lead character’s name and the play’s title.
Purlie Victorious manages to have fun without shying away from the historical reality of Black oppression.
Leslie Odom, Jr. and Kara Young are both dazzlingly funny and incredibly warm in these roles as are the rest of a superb cast.
Fortunately, the new production of Ossie Davis’ 1961 play Purlie Victorious has sidestepped any issues about its being dated for two reasons, one good and one bad.
The wisdom is that humanity triumphs through comedy delivered with love which builds community and heals the tremendous pain of oppression.
As deft as the acting is, the audience also winds up toggling – between the (sometimes outdated) comedy of the plot and the (often still timely) underlying outrage.

cn.t: Critics hail this long-overdue revival of Ossie Davis's 1961 satire as hilarious and bracingly relevant, with stellar performances from Leslie Odom Jr. and Kara Young elevating Kenny Leon's energetic, breakneck production of a comedy that still resonates today.

sg.ra: In a 1,023-seat house, rows E-L are the Goldilocks zone: close enough to read faces, far enough to take the whole set at once without the neck strain that rows A-B force under this unusually high stage.
A strong alternate to center orchestra — elevated, unobstructed, and closer than most mezz sections in a small house. Stay center; side seats face jutting boxes.

This is the small-house dividend: rows M-O still feel detailed at Music Box scale and cost less than the prime band. Skip row P if your show has a tall set, where the mezz overhang starts clipping the top.
A strong rake and a small footprint mean the back of the mezz still reads the stage cleanly here. Worth it if you'd rather spend the money on two shows than one.
The Music Box stage sits high, so these rows put you looking up for two hours and missing upstage blocking. Sources recommend them conditionally at best — skip unless proximity is the whole point.

vr.q: Overall, I think this play was really worth reviving, and I would definitely recommend going. It's funny, it's well paced, it's well acted, and it's under two hours with no intermission, which I love.
Overall, this was an enjoyable play. I'm glad they revive this play, and this is a very strong start to our play revival race this season.
